title: ESI Triage & Alert Time Goals
body:
## The ESI decision points

**A.** Dying? → ESI `1`. **B.** Should not wait? → ESI `2`. **C.** How many resources? → `2` or more = ESI `3`, one = ESI `4`, none = ESI `5`. **D.** Before settling on `3`, check the danger-zone vitals — abnormal ones push it up to `2`.

| Level | Definition | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **1** | Needs an immediate life-saving intervention | Cardiac or respiratory arrest, apnea, unresponsive, severe respiratory distress with `SpO2` under `90%`, anaphylaxis, hypotension with poor perfusion, major trauma in shock, intubated arrival |
| **2** | High risk, or confused/lethargic/disoriented, or severe pain or distress (`7–10` with a matching picture) | Chest pain suspicious for ACS, stroke symptoms, suicidal or homicidal ideation, neutropenic fever, DKA, ectopic pregnancy, sickle cell crisis, sudden worst-headache, sexual assault, infant under `28 d` with fever |
| **3** | Two or more resources, stable vitals | Abdominal pain needing labs, CT and IV medication; new-onset vomiting with labs plus IV fluids |
| **4** | One resource | Laceration needing sutures, wrist injury needing an X-ray, simple UTI needing a urinalysis |
| **5** | No resources | Prescription refill, suture removal, simple rash needing only a prescription, work note |

## Danger-zone vitals (step D)

Any one of these on an otherwise ESI `3` patient makes you consider upgrading to ESI `2`.

| Age | HR above | RR above |
|---|---|---|
| Under `3 mo` | `180` | `50` |
| `3 mo – 3 y` | `160` | `40` |
| `3 – 8 y` | `140` | `30` |
| Over `8 y` and adults | `100` | `20` |

`SpO2` under `92%` at any age is a danger-zone value. Fever rules: any infant under `28 d` with a temp of `38.0 C` (`100.4 F`) is ESI `2`; `1–3 mo` with fever is at least a strong ESI `2` consideration; `3 mo – 3 y` with `39 C` (`102.2 F`) and no source or incomplete immunizations is at least ESI `3`.

## Counting resources

Count each **type** once, not each order.

| Counts as a resource | Does **not** count |
|---|---|
| Labs (all blood and urine together = `1`) | History and physical, including a pelvic exam |
| ECG | Point-of-care testing |
| Plain X-rays (all = `1`) | Saline or heparin lock |
| Advanced imaging: CT, MRI, ultrasound, angiography (all together = `1`) | Oral medications |
| IV fluids for hydration | Tetanus immunization |
| IV, IM or nebulized medication | Prescription refill |
| Specialty consultation | Phone call to the primary provider |
| Simple procedure (laceration repair, Foley) = `1` | Simple wound care: dressings, recheck |
| Complex procedure (procedural sedation) = `2` | Crutches, splints, slings |

Example: abdominal pain getting labs, a CT and IV ondansetron = `3` resources, so ESI `3`. Ankle injury getting an X-ray and an ACE wrap = `1` resource (the wrap does not count), so ESI `4`.

> **Trap:** The resource count is a prediction of what a **prudent provider** would order, not a count of what got ordered. You make it at triage, before anyone writes an order.

## Line-jumping complaints

Bring these straight back regardless of how busy the waiting room is: chest pain or suspected ACS, stroke symptoms, airway compromise or severe respiratory distress, uncontrolled bleeding, altered mental status, hypotension or sepsis criteria, anaphylaxis, testicular pain (torsion) or priapism, chemical eye splash (irrigate before you finish triage), vaginal bleeding or abdominal pain in pregnancy, active labor, suicidal or homicidal ideation, neutropenic or immunocompromised fever, fever in an infant under `28 d`, sickle cell pain crisis, snakebite, and any acute limb ischemia.

## Alert time goals

| Alert | Target |
|---|---|
| **STEMI** door-to-ECG | `10 min` from arrival, interpreted by a physician immediately |
| STEMI door-to-balloon (PCI) | `90 min` at a PCI-capable center; `120 min` if transferring out |
| STEMI door-to-needle (fibrinolytic, no PCI available) | `30 min` |
| **Stroke** door-to-provider | `10 min` |
| Stroke door-to-stroke-team | `15 min` |
| Stroke door-to-CT (scan started) | `25 min`; read by `45 min` |
| Stroke door-to-needle (thrombolytic) | `60 min`, many centers now target `45 min` |
| IV thrombolytic window | `4.5 h` from last known well |
| Mechanical thrombectomy window | up to `24 h` from last known well in selected large-vessel occlusions with favorable imaging |
| **Sepsis** 1-hour bundle | Measure lactate; draw blood cultures **before** antibiotics; give broad-spectrum antibiotics; start `30 mL/kg` crystalloid for hypotension or lactate `4` or more; add vasopressors for `MAP` at least `65` if still hypotensive; remeasure lactate |

Bundle timing is measured from the time of sepsis recognition, and hospitals define that trigger slightly differently.

## Typical full trauma activation criteria

SBP under `90` (under `110` if age `65` or older), GCS `8` or less with trauma, penetrating injury to head, neck, torso or proximal extremity, gunshot wound to neck, chest or abdomen, respiratory compromise or an intubated arrival, transfer patient receiving blood, amputation proximal to the wrist or ankle, two or more proximal long-bone fractures, flail chest, paralysis, crushed or mangled extremity, unstable pelvis, and physician discretion.

> **On shift:** Activation criteria and tier names are **set by each trauma center** and each state's field triage plan. Learn your own department's card — the list above is the common core, not a universal rule.
